questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of fever, myalgia, and headache. She worked on a farm near Savannah, Georgia. Though she did not recall any recent rashes or illness, she removed at least two ticks from her skin in the past month. She had a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes. She was taking losartan, metformin, and gliclazide. On examination, the patient appeared ill. Her temperature was 39.3°C (102.7°F); other vital signs were normal. Examination was otherwise unremarkable. Investigations: Total white cell count 2.3 ×109/L Platelet count 92 ×109/L ALT 84 U/L Peripheral blood smear:
questions.lead_in: What organism is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Ehrlichia chaffeensis HME, or ehrlichiosis, is caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, an intracellular pathogen that infects monocytes. The image shows morulae within monocytes. This is diagnostic for HME.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q31

questions.question: You are asked to see a woman in her 40s who lives in Montreal and who has never traveled. She presented with fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, and migratory arthralgias. She also developed a maculopapular rash on her extremities that became petechial and purpuric. She was seen in the ER 5 days ago. See picture of her rash and Gram stain of her blood culture.
questions.question_raw: You are asked to see a woman in her 40's who lives in Montreal and who has never traveled. She presented with fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, and migratory arthralgias. She also developed a maculopapular rash on her extremities that became petechial and purpuric. She was seen in the ER 5 days ago. See picture of her rash and Gram stain of her blood culture.

parts.text: What one epidemiological question do you ask her?
What is the organism? Name to species level.
If this was suspected on initial presentation, why should the microbiology lab be notified?

parts_raw.text: What ONE epidemiological question do you ask her?
What is the organism? Name to species level.
If this was suspected on initial presentation, why should the microbiology lab be notified?

questions.model_answer:
a) Has she had contact with a Neisseria meningitidis case or been in a crowded/closed setting, or completed meningococcal vaccination? (i.e., ask about exposure to a known meningococcal case / vaccination status.)
b) Neisseria meningitidis (gram-negative diplococci on Gram stain, with fever and petechial/purpuric rash = meningococcemia).
c) N. meningitidis is a risk to laboratory personnel; alerting the lab allows biosafety precautions (handling in a biosafety cabinet) and prompts consideration of post-exposure prophylaxis for exposed staff, and expedites identification.
d) IV third-generation cephalosporin: ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h (or cefotaxime); plus droplet precautions and public-health notification with chemoprophylaxis (rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone) for close contacts.

questions.question: Otherwise healthy 17-year-old male with a painful and pruritic rash on the hands and feet, well demarcated at the wrists and ankles.
questions.question_raw: Otherwise healthy 17 M with painful and pruritic rash on hands and feet, well demarcated at wrists and ankles

parts.text: One simple investigation to confirm the diagnosis.

parts_raw.text: One simple investigation to confirm dx?

questions.model_answer:
a) Papular-purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS), most often associated with parvovirus B19; self-limited over 1-2 weeks.
b) Serum parvovirus B19 IgM (and IgG) serology.

cohort_answer.text: Papular-purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) - 2/3 assoc with parvovirus B19, sporadically VZV/EBV/CMV/HSV6-7/Coxsackie/HepB/Rubella; self-resolving 7-14 days. Investigation: IgM parvovirus B19 (positive up to 2-3 months post-infection), can also check IgG avidity

questions.question: A woman travels to Tanzania and climbs Mount Kilimanjaro. She presents with fever and an eschar. List 3 organisms on the differential.
questions.question_raw: A woman travels to Tanzania and climbs Mount Kilimanjaro. She presents with a fever and eschar.
questions.model_answer: (1) Rickettsia africae (African tick-bite fever) - the leading cause of fever with eschar in sub-Saharan Africa travelers; produces multiple inoculation eschars. (2) Francisella tularensis (ulceroglandular tularaemia) - eschar/ulcer with regional lymphadenopathy. (3) Bacillus anthracis (cutaneous anthrax) - painless black eschar. (Scrub typhus, Orientia tsutsugamushi, is an alternative but is not endemic to this region.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Only R. africae is grounded in this chapter (Table 185.3, sub-Saharan Africa, 100% multiple eschars); tularaemia and anthrax as eschar causes are from standard travel/ID sources (IDSA, CDC Yellow Book), not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: African trypanosomiasis; Tularemia; Rickettsia africae (African tick bite fever); Scrub typhus; Bacillus anthracis; Plague.

questions.question: [image-based question: picture of a tick, appears to be Dermacentor]
questions.question_raw: [image-based question: picture of a tick, looked like Dermacentor]

parts.text: Name one infection associated with this tick.

parts_raw.text: Name 1 infection associated with this tick.

questions.model_answer: a) Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii). Dermacentor spp. (D. variabilis, the American dog tick, and D. andersoni, the Rocky Mountain wood tick) are the principal vectors; other acceptable Dermacentor-associated infections include tularemia, Colorado tick fever, and tick paralysis.
